title: You don't need science to see results
summary: NH argues you can make big gains without scientific knowledge, as he did in his first five years, because the body is the teacher. Beyond a basic threshold (technique and form from basic creators like Omar Isuf and Alan Thrall), more literature adds little. He criticises science-obsessed fitness for producing timid, smug lifters who over-control variables and under-work, and says his channel is experience-based.

claims.claim: You can absolutely get bigger and more muscular without scientific knowledge of lifting; for his first ~5 years he progressed doing whatever he wanted, following bro science from the internet and anime/manga.
Part of that is that novices gain from almost anything.
The human body didn't wait for science to grow; many big, strong natural gym bros never read exercise science. Your body is the teacher and the source of what studies measure.
Learning only from your body means making many mistakes and possibly leaving gains on the table.
Many science-obsessed fitness people don't look like they lift; they treat exercise science like math and don't seek empirical evidence on their own bodies, which he sees as a waste.
There's a threshold of knowledge needed to be optimal, mainly technique and proper form adapted to your body; beyond it, extra literature is a bonus that may not be useful.

Form knowledge is mostly found on basic content creators, not peer-reviewed studies; he learned squat, deadlift, bench and OHP from Omar Isuf's and Alan Thrall's early channels, then built his own knowledge.
Time spent reading a 20-page paper on biceps activation would be better spent curling; the best arms belong to gym bros who curl to failure and go up in weight without overthinking.
Developing discipline and love for the iron is more desirable than loving theory; detailed theory is for advanced lifters seeking small edges.
He made his best gains knowing nothing about squat angles, protein timing or optimal volume, and believes knowing it would have made him too timid with the weights.
Science-based YouTube fitness is making people afraid to act and over-control variables so they work less; he predicts a regression in gains. There is no 'perfect workout'.
Older channels taught 'here's how to squat, now get to work'; today's are too theoretical, and theory is only a small part of training.
Knowledge is making a new generation of lifters smug: they think they've found the truth but can't show results.
A natural with a good physique is a mine of knowledge that, while not peer-reviewed, is just as valuable; his channel shares experience, not science.
